title: Fats & Oils
subtitle: 1960–today · Soy, Palm and the Fat Wars: The Tropical Oils War, Trans Fats, Olestra, the Whaling Moratorium, Olive-Oil Fraud and the Palm Frontier

entries.label: Soybean growers and health campaigners declare war on palm and coconut oil
entries.hint: As Malaysian palm oil made inroads in the United States — US consumption rose 158 per cent between 1981 and 1985 — the American Soybean Association launched a media campaign in 1986 branding it an ‘unhealthy tropical grease’; Sokolof’s newspaper advertisements against ‘tropical oils’ ran in 1988, the year of the Center for Science in the Public Interest’s booklet Saturated Fat Attack. Malaysian counter-advertising of 1989 stressed that palm oil needed no hydrogenation, but by 1989 General Mills, Quaker Oats, Borden, Pepperidge Farm, Keebler, Purina and Pillsbury had announced they would drop tropical oils, which usually meant replacing them with partially hydrogenated soybean oil.
entries.note: SECONDARY (two books read; both partisan in this fight): Zuckerman, Planet Palm (2021), the tropical-oils passage (US consumption +158 per cent, 1981–85; the ASA’s 1986 ad); Teicholz, The Big Fat Surprise (2014) ch.8 (the Sokolof advertisement of 1 November 1988; the ASA’s 1986–89 campaign under Drake; Ronk’s 1987 testimony; the 1989 company announcements). Teicholz argues the campaign’s claims were ‘inaccurate’; the science of palm oil’s saturated fat and heart disease remains debated.

entries.label: The “Olive Wars” of the West Bank: groves burned, uprooted and cut off, 2000–2010
entries.hint: Mueller reports that after the Six-Day War of 1967 the West Bank held an estimated ten million olive trees owned by Palestinian farmers, and that from 2000, the year of the Second Intifada, Israeli soldiers and Jewish settlers, citing security concerns, began to burn, cut down and uproot olive trees, particularly near roads, settlements and the borders with Jordan and Syria; some sources put the destruction at up to half a million Palestinian-owned trees, in what the liberal Israeli press calls the Olive Wars, and the barrier built since October 2005 has put more groves off limits. Settlers have been accused of stealing olives. An Israeli archaeologist told him that people on both sides plant olives to control the land. He also describes Christians caught up in the conflict, and a priest’s account of Muslims and Christians in a Christian-Muslim town harvesting side by side and bringing a bottle of first oil to the church for the sacrament.
entries.note: CONTESTED (journalistic account; figures are Mueller’s, from unnamed ‘sources’, and the political claims are disputed): Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011), the chapters on the Holy Land (PDF pp.120–125 of the extraction). Compare fats-1200bc-300bc::b5 for Tekoa’s oil for the Temple, which Mueller sets in the same hills.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Dietary Goals, trans-fat rules, olestra, the olive standard, the whaling moratorium and biofuel mandates

entries.label: The McGovern committee’s Dietary Goals: eat less fat
entries.hint: The Senate Select Committee on Nutrition, chaired by George McGovern, issued Dietary Goals for the United States in 1977, urging Americans to eat less fat and cholesterol, and the Surgeon General’s report of 1979 backed it; the committee had heard in 1976 that fat might cause cancer, and the 1977 hearings gave Harvard’s nutrition professor Fredrick Stare a platform. Teicholz argues the advice shaped four decades of American policy on weak evidence.
entries.note: SECONDARY (journalistic account read): Teicholz (2014) ch.2 and ch.6 and notes (Select Committee on Nutrition and Human Needs, Dietary Goals for the United States (GPO, 1977); the Surgeon General’s report of 1979). The 1988 first Surgeon General’s Report on Nutrition and Health, which Nestle edited, is described in Nestle, Food Politics (2013 ed.) Introduction. The scientific status of the advice is contested.

entries.label: The IWC bans commercial whaling
entries.hint: In 1982 the International Whaling Commission passed a moratorium on all commercial whaling, after quotas for minke whales had been cut every year from 1977; by then, Ellis says, the whalers had already destroyed most of the whales, and the grass-roots movement behind the moratorium began only about 1972. Japan went on killing sperm whales after the moratorium.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis, Men and Whales (1991) pp.xvi, 27 and 314 (PDF pp.19, 50, 337). The moratorium’s effective date (1986) and the later history are not in the passages read.

entries.label: The FDA approves Olestra, one day before its patent would have expired
entries.hint: Procter & Gamble developed sucrose polyester (olestra), a fat that passes through the body unabsorbed, in 1968; after a Congress-granted patent extension that ran to 25 January 1996 if the FDA approved the product by then, the agency approved olestra for savoury snacks on 24 January 1996, with provisos including a warning notice. P&G and Frito-Lay released Olean snacks nationwide in 1998; the Center for Science in the Public Interest had opposed it since 1987.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Nestle, Food Politics (2013 ed.), the chapter on olestra and its chronology table, ‘Key events in the history of the approval and marketing of olestra, 1968–2003’.

entries.label: Denmark limits trans fats; the FDA requires them on the label
entries.hint: In 2003 Denmark passed the first national trans-fat limit, allowing no more than 2 per cent trans fat as a share of total fat; the US FDA adopted a labelling rule in 2003 that required trans fats to have their own line on the Nutrition Facts panel of packaged foods from 1 January 2006. Willett’s Nurses’ Health Study paper of 1993 in The Lancet and the 1994 petition of the Center for Science in the Public Interest were the scientific and campaigning roots.
entries.note: SECONDARY (journalistic account read): Teicholz (2014) ch.8 (the Danish law; the FDA rule of 2003 and the 2006 compliance date; Willett 1993; CSPI’s 1994 petition; Mensink & Katan’s trial). On the strength of the evidence she is sceptical of the epidemiology but not of the case against industrial trans fats.

entries.label: Federal marshals seize 87,000 litres of “extra virgin” oil in New Jersey
entries.hint: In 2006, in a rare intervention, federal marshals seized about 61,000 litres of supposedly extra virgin olive oil and 26,000 litres of olive pomace oil from a New Jersey warehouse; in 1997 they had seized an olive pomace oil brand that turned out to be partly or wholly sunflower oil. Canada’s food inspection agency, testing retail olive oils from 1997, has found over 20 per cent of them fraudulent.
entries.note: SECONDARY (journalistic account; allegations of fraud not adjudicated): Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011), the chapters on fraud in the United States (the 2006 seizure; the Krinos pomace seizure of 1997; the Canadian Food Inspection Agency’s tests).

entries.label: Renewable-fuel mandates turn palm oil into diesel
entries.hint: The US Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 required 36 billion gallons of renewable fuels by 2022, from corn, soy, oil palm and sugar; the European Union followed with its own targets and became the second-largest palm-oil importer after India. By 2017 oil palm provided 31 per cent of the world’s biofuel feedstock, and Indonesia, which introduced a 20 per cent blending rule in 2016, later raised it to 40 per cent and added a power-generation mandate.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; not checked against statutes): Zuckerman, Planet Palm (2021), the chapter on biofuels (EISA 2007; EU imports; the 31 per cent figure from a 2020 news analysis; Indonesia’s 2016 rule, ‘now raised it to 40 percent’).

entries.label: The USDA updates the olive-oil standard, 2010 — voluntary and unenforced
entries.hint: In October 2010 the USDA finally replaced its trade standard for olive oil, which dated from 1948, with one mirroring the International Olive Council’s; it remained voluntary, with no provision for enforcement, in a country whose olive-oil consumption was third in the world and growing 10 per cent a year. A UC Davis study that year reported widespread mislabelling of ‘extra virgin’ oil, and a class action followed against Unilever, Carapelli and Sysco, among others.
entries.note: SECONDARY (journalistic account; both claims unadjudicated): Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011), the chapters on fraud in the United States (the USDA update, the UC Davis study of 2010, the class action of August 2010). Mueller is an advocate for quality oil; the study’s methods and the lawsuit’s outcome were not checked.

entries.label: The FDA moves to ban partially hydrogenated oils; the WHO plans to end them
entries.hint: In late 2013, partly in response to a petition from the biochemist Fred Kummerow, then 98, the FDA proposed banning all trans fats; in 2018 the WHO launched an initiative to eliminate artificial trans-fatty acids from the world’s food supply by 2023. Palm oil’s semi-solid texture made it the favoured swap-in for the partially hydrogenated oils.
entries.note: SECONDARY (two books read): Teicholz (2014) ch.8 (the FDA’s proposal of 2013, Kummerow’s petition; as of 2014 the agency was ‘on the verge’) and Zuckerman (2021) (the WHO initiative of 2018 for 2023; palm as the substitute). The outcome of the FDA’s action and of the WHO plan after the books’ publication was not checked.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Palmolive’s 1966 line and the 1988 anti-tropical-oil advertisements

entries.label: “You’re soaking in it”: Madge the manicurist and Palmolive
entries.hint: The Palmolive dish-detergent campaign of 1966, with the manicurist Madge’s line ‘You’re soaking in it’, unwittingly prefigured what palm oil would become: US palm-oil imports rose from 29,000 metric tons in 1966 to more than 1.5 million, and by 263 per cent in the last fifteen years before the book’s writing, thanks partly to the FDA’s trans-fat measures.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history): Zuckerman, Planet Palm (2021), Prologue (the Palmolive tagline and campaign of 1966; the import figures). The match of the advertisement’s date with the import figures is Zuckerman’s device, not evidence of cause.

entries.label: Newspaper advertisements against “tropical oils”
entries.hint: A series of full-page advertisements in national newspapers in the 1980s, among them one in the New York Times on 1 November 1988, portrayed tropical oils as a threat to health. Teicholz judges them to have been inaccurate, and says that Malaysian palm-oil interests answered in 1989 with ads of their own, copying the tactic.
entries.note: SECONDARY (journalistic account read): Teicholz (2014) ch.8, the Sokolof advertisement of 1 November 1988 and the 1989 Ong counter-ads. Her judgment of the claims is hers.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The trans-fat evidence and the Women’s Health Initiative

entries.label: Mensink and Katan, then Willett: trans fats named as a danger
entries.hint: A clinical trial by Mensink and Katan (published in 1990) found that trans fats raised ‘bad’ cholesterol; Walter Willett’s Nurses’ Health Study data, which Mary Enig’s work had led him to collect for 90,000 nurses from 1980, showed in a 1993 Lancet paper a correlation between trans-fat intake and heart disease, and in 1994 he and a colleague estimated that trans fats caused 30,000 American deaths a year. The Harvard press release made the point plain; CSPI petitioned the FDA the same year.
entries.note: SECONDARY (journalistic account read; the papers not read): Teicholz (2014) ch.8 (Mensink and Katan’s year, 1990, is not given in the passage read). She notes that the 30,000-death figure rested on epidemiological correlations that had not been confirmed by trials, and that Unilever had announced in 1992 that it would remove partially hydrogenated oils from most of its products within three years — years before the labelling rule.

entries.label: The Women’s Health Initiative finds no benefit from a low-fat diet
entries.hint: The Women’s Health Initiative enrolled 49,000 women in 1993, expecting to validate the benefits of a low-fat diet once and for all; after a decade of more fruit, vegetables and whole grains and less meat and fat, the women did not lose weight and saw no significant reduction in heart disease or any major cancer. Teicholz calls it the largest and longest trial of the low-fat diet, whose results showed it had ‘quite simply failed’; its defenders dispute her reading.
entries.note: CONTESTED (journalistic reading of a trial not read): Teicholz (2014) introduction and ch.5 (Women’s Health Initiative; JAMA papers of 2006). The WHI’s own investigators drew narrower conclusions about the specific diet intervention than Teicholz does; the trial is cited here as an episode in the dispute, not as a verdict.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Soybean oil, Malaysia’s palm boom, India’s imports, the American palm market, olive oil’s new world, the end of whale oil

entries.label: Soybean oil becomes the world’s most-used oil — and America’s hydrogenated one
entries.hint: In the last half-century soybean oil, once a minor oil, became the most widely used of all; palm has grown dramatically in recent decades, and soybean, palm, sunflower and rapeseed oils now lead world production. Teicholz says Americans consumed more than 18 billion pounds of soybean oil by 2001 — over 80 per cent of all oils eaten in the United States — most of it partially hydrogenated and so loaded with trans fats; vegetable oils grew from zero to nearly 8 per cent of American calories over a century.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly chapter and journalistic account read): Kiple, Cambridge World History of Food (2000) II.E.1 p.375 (PDF p.412: soybean oil ‘by far the leader, followed by palm, sunflower and rapeseed’; palm’s rapid growth); Teicholz (2014) ch.8 and introduction (the 18 billion pounds and 80 per cent; the share of calories). The ‘more than 80 per cent’ is Teicholz’s own figure.

entries.label: Whale oil ends: the last whaling for profit
entries.hint: After the war the whaling industry kept supplying oil — 211,650 sperm whales were killed outside the Antarctic in the decade 1961–71 — until the quotas of the 1970s, the 1982 moratorium and the competition of vegetable oils ended it. Ellis’s history closes with chapters on ‘the end of whaling for profit’.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis, Men and Whales (1991) p.319 (PDF p.342; the 1961–71 sperm whale kills) and his chapter list (PDF p.13). The role of vegetable-oil competition in ending whaling is the folio’s reading of the earlier folios, not Ellis’s statement in the passage read.

entries.label: FELDA and Tenera: Malaysia replants rubber with oil palm
entries.hint: Malaysia’s oil-palm development was more rapid than Indonesia’s after 1945, especially after 1960, when the replanting of old rubber estates with oil palms was stimulated by the smallholder schemes of FELDA, the Federal Land Development Authority; large-scale Tenera breeding began after 1945, and in Indonesia the area under oil palm rose from 90,000 hectares in government schemes in 1971 to 310,000 in 1985, with 100,000 hectares of smallholders by then.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly chapter with a table): Kiple, Cambridge World History of Food (2000) II.E.3 p.399 (PDF p.436, Table II.E.3.1, from Hartley 1988 and Taniputra et al. 1988). The table’s totals are inconsistent in the printed text and only the government-scheme and smallholder figures are used.

entries.label: Japan adds meat, dairy products, fats and oils to a rice diet, from the 1960s
entries.hint: Ishige describes rice as the chief feature of the Japanese diet, and a source of both carbohydrate and protein, from its introduction some two millennia ago until the 1960s, a time of great change in eating patterns when large amounts of meat, dairy products and fats and oils began to be eaten and both the amount of rice consumed and its importance as a protein source began to decline. Nutritionists had observed that in pre-modern times the Japanese diet was deficient in protein, oils and fats.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Ishige (2001), PDF pp.32 and 150 (the nutritionists’ observation, on the Ryukyu Islands, where fat from lard was eaten). Ishige gives no figures in these passages; the decade is his ‘the 1960s’.

entries.label: India’s vanaspati under price control: Unilever’s margin falls to 4 per cent
entries.hint: In India, Kiple notes, there is a large consumer demand for vanaspati, a shortening developed as a replacement for butterfat ghee, and similar shortenings are traditional in Pakistan, Egypt and other Middle Eastern countries, which often import palm products from Malaysia ready processed. Jones adds that in the 1960s Unilever’s profits from vanaspati fell away: government controls on imported raw materials kept vegetable-oil prices artificially high, reducing vanaspati’s cheapness against natural ghee, while price controls cut Unilever’s gross margin to only 4 per cent, and by the early 1970s the business was completely unprofitable. The company could not withdraw from a mass-consumption article without the government’s anger.
entries.note: ANCHOR (books read): Jones, Renewing Unilever (2005) PDF pp.189–190; Kiple (2000) II.E.3 p.407 (PDF p.444). Compare fats-1900-1960::ec12 for vanaspati’s rise.

entries.label: Malaysia’s palm-oil boom: output twenty-five-fold in twenty years
entries.hint: Between 1964 and 1984, while Malaysia partially nationalised its plantations sector, its palm-oil production grew more than twenty-five-fold; in 1974 United Plantations opened Malaysia’s first industrial palm-oil refinery; and in 2019 the industry produced a record 20.5 million tonnes worth some $9 billion. Worldwide, the availability of palm oil rose 206 per cent between 1961 and 2009.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history): Zuckerman, Planet Palm (2021), the chapters on Malaysia (the 25-fold, the 1974 refinery, the 2019 record, the 206 per cent). The Malaysian side is detailed in Martin, The UP Saga (2003), which was not read for the post-1960 chapters.

entries.label: The Middle East takes its fat as imported palm oil: Egypt 330,000 tonnes by 1990
entries.loc: Egypt, Iraq, Turkey and Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: Kiple writes that vanaspati, the shortening developed in India as a replacement for butterfat ghee, has counterparts that are traditional in Pakistan, Egypt and other Middle Eastern countries, and that such countries, often lacking refining facilities of their own, tended to import palm-oil products from Malaysia in fully processed, ready-to-eat form. Malaysia encouraged this with tax concessions for refineries and a remission of the export tax on crude palm oil that grew with the degree of processing of the product. His table of palm-oil imports in thousand tonnes a year shows Egypt at 330 in 1990, Iraq at 110 in 1980 and 220 in 1990, Turkey at 200 and Saudi Arabia at 110 and 130, against 630 for India, 680 for Pakistan, 1,600 for Western Europe and 8,440 for the world.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Berger’s ‘Palm Oil’ chapter in Kiple & Ornelas, eds., The Cambridge World History of Food (2000), PDF p.444 and Table II.E.3.8, citing Mielke (1988, 1991) and Amiruddin and Ahmad (1984). The table gives no figure for Egypt, Turkey or Saudi Arabia before 1980 or 1990, and its dashes may mean no data rather than no imports; the traditions of fat in these countries are not described.

entries.label: The new olive-oil world: California, Australia and the American market
entries.hint: Olive oil was revived in new countries from the 1990s: a group of northern Californians, including Ed Stolman, started an oil press in 1995; Australian growers set a new quality agenda; and by 2009 America had overtaken Greece as the world’s third-largest consumer of olive oil, though the average American ate only 0.9 litres a year, half the Australian figure and 4 per cent of the Greek.
entries.note: SECONDARY (journalistic account read): Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011), the final chapters on new worlds of oil (consumption figures; the Stolman group of 1995). Mueller cites consumption from the trade, not an official statistic.

entries.label: India becomes the world’s largest buyer of palm oil
entries.hint: India, now the world’s number-one palm-oil importer, went from buying 30,000 tonnes in 1992 to 9.2 million in 2019; Mexico’s imports rose more than fivefold from 1995; and global consumption reached nearly 72 million tonnes, some twenty pounds a head. A Stanford study of 2013 estimated that a 20 per cent tax on palm oil in India would avert about 363,000 deaths from heart disease over ten years.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history): Zuckerman (2021) Prologue and the chapters on India (30,000 t to 9.2 million; Basu 2013 for the tax estimate; Mexico). Zuckerman’s ‘nearly 72 million tonnes’ is for the year before her writing, i.e. about 2019–20.

entries.label: The trans-fat ban gives palm oil an American market
entries.hint: Palm oil’s semi-solid texture at room temperature made it the ideal swap-in for the partially hydrogenated oils used in cookies and crackers: US imports rose 263 per cent in fifteen years, to more than 1.5 million tonnes, ‘thanks in part to’ the FDA’s trans-fat rules, and American companies imported some 2.5 billion pounds in 2012, about five times as much as in the 1980s when soybean growers had launched their anti-tropical-oil campaign. Teicholz adds that restaurants’ switch to polyunsaturated frying oils created its own concern about heated oils.
entries.note: SECONDARY (two books read): Zuckerman (2021) Prologue (263 per cent; palm as swap-in); Teicholz (2014) ch.8 (the 2.5 billion pounds in 2012, five times the 1980s; the frying-oil concern, Ryther 2007). The frying-oil danger is Teicholz’s claim and was not examined.

entries.label: Olestra: a fat the body cannot absorb
entries.hint: Procter & Gamble researchers discovered sucrose polyester, olestra, a sugar–fatty-acid compound with the sensory properties of fat that retains its taste but passes through the body unabsorbed, by accident in 1968; it was approved in 1996 for savoury snacks and sold as Olean from 1998. By 1998 P&G estimated that Americans had eaten 28 million olestra snacks, ‘saving’ over two billion calories and 285 tons of fat.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Nestle, Food Politics (2013 ed.), the olestra chapter, including P&G’s own estimate (a company claim).

entries.label: Canada breeds a rapeseed fit to eat: “canola”
entries.hint: Canadian researchers Baldur Stefansson and Keith Downey bred rapeseed low in erucic acid, first for oil and then for meal, and the crop was renamed canola; the oil, from a plant that had been a lamp oil and a lubricant in Europe since the Middle Ages, became a mainstream food oil in North America.
entries.note: UNVERIFIED (thin lead; web summaries only): found through a web search of canola histories (a university extension page and Canola Council material); the library has no source on canola’s breeding. Dates are given loosely for the decade because the summaries did not fix them. Kiple, II.E.1 p.378, lists rapeseed (canola) at 35–60 per cent oil.

entries.label: High-oleic sunflower oil from Russia, the 1970s
entries.hint: High-oleic sunflower oils originated in Russia in the mid-1970s through selective breeding and mutagenesis, the original line ‘Pervenets’; it was later developed into lines with a stable high oleic-acid composition. Kiple counts it among the genetic changes that have altered the fatty acid composition of oilseeds, alongside a general displacement of animal fats by plant oils.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly chapter): Kiple (2000) II.E.1 p.383 (PDF p.420, citing Morrison, Hamilton & Kalu 1994 for ‘Prevenets’, a different transliteration from the one given here) and p.376 (PDF p.413).

entries.label: Turkish hazelnut oil becomes “Greek olive oil” at Barletta, 1991: investigators’ account
entries.hint: Italian investigators told Mueller that on 10 August 1991 a rusty tanker, the Mazal II, loaded 2,200 tons of hazelnut oil at the Turkish port of Ordu and wandered through the Mediterranean and North Sea; when it reached Barletta in Puglia on 21 September its cargo had become, on the ship’s documents, Greek olive oil. Between August and November 1991 two tankers delivered nearly 10,000 tons of Turkish hazelnut oil and Argentinian sunflower oil to an Italian refinery, all identified as Greek olive oil, according to the investigators; the refiner’s own account of events differs.
entries.note: CONTESTED (journalistic account of allegations, not adjudicated): Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011), the chapter on the Puglia investigations; the refiner told Mueller another story. No individual is named here for that reason. Compare x2 and o8.

entries.label: Tunisian oil into Puglia: allegations of non-EU oil passed off as Italian
entries.hint: Mueller reports Italian investigators alleging that a Puglia importer evaded more than €22 million in EU duties between 1998 and 2004 by illegally importing 17,000 tons of Turkish and Tunisian olive oil; in an earlier case Italy’s Supreme Court noted, in January 1997, a magistrate’s finding that a cargo unloaded at Monopoli was non-EU olive oil from Tunisia, free of import tariffs, then made to look Italian by false sales. An oil-fraud investigator named Sfax among the Mediterranean towns where bogus extra virgins were made. Charges against the importer and his associates were later dismissed on the statute of limitations. Tunisia appears here as a cheap supplier whose oil is relabelled, not as a brand.
entries.note: CONTESTED (journalistic account of allegations, not adjudicated): Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011), the chapters on the ‘Mediterranean Axis’ plan and the Puglia investigations (the €22 million and 17,000-ton figures are investigators’ claims as Mueller reports them; the 1997 ruling; the dismissal). Compare o8 and l3.

entries.label: A global supply chain: Wilmar, Cargill and the palm refiners
entries.hint: Wilmar trades some 40 per cent of the world’s palm oil, and a Greenpeace International report found that eighteen of the mills supplying it were linked to deforestation, in violation of its 2013 NDPE (no deforestation, no peat, no exploitation) policy. Golden Agri-Resources, whose buyers include Nestlé, Procter & Gamble and Unilever, was accused in March 2020 of operating plantations illegally inside Indonesia’s protected forest zones; PepsiCo bought 485,756 tonnes and McDonald’s 92,534 tonnes of palm oil in 2019.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; allegations as reported, not adjudicated): Zuckerman, Planet Palm (2021), chapters on the supply chain and consumer-goods buyers; the Greenpeace and NGO reports are cited there, and the companies’ replies were not examined.

entries.label: The 2015 fires: six million acres of forest burn
entries.hint: In the summer and fall of 2015, fires traced to oil-palm plantations across Sumatra and Borneo burned more than 6 million acres of forest, an area larger than Vermont; tropical deforestation is responsible for about 8 per cent of annual greenhouse-gas emissions, more than the whole European Union. The 2004 Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil and company pledges to end deforestation were the industry’s reply.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; the figures cited from NGO and agency reports): Zuckerman (2021), the later chapters and Epilogue. The founding date of the RSPO (2004) is common knowledge, not stated in the passage read, and is given here as a marker only.

entries.label: The toxic oil syndrome: rapeseed oil sold as olive oil kills 800 in Spain
entries.hint: In 1981 in Spain, rapeseed oil adulterated with an industrial additive and sold as olive oil caused the toxic oil syndrome, killing about eight hundred people and seriously injuring thousands more — the worst case in the history of olive-oil fraud and a reminder that cheap oils had long been passed as olive.
entries.note: SECONDARY (journalistic account): Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011), the chapter on fraud (‘the 1981 case of toxic oil syndrome in Spain’). Later epidemiological studies were not consulted; the outbreak was in fact attributed to aniline-denatured rapeseed oil, which the passage describes only as an ‘industrial additive’.

entries.label: Plantation workers and villagers: from Sumatra to Cameroon and Honduras
entries.hint: Since 2011 communities around the plantations of Socfin, the company founded by Adrien Hallet, have sought reparations in Cameroon and Sierra Leone for land acquisitions and working conditions; in 2013 a delegation of Socapalm workers travelled to Paris. In Honduras and Guatemala farmers have been pushed from fertile land, and in 2017 workers of Agroguay and Agromeza joined a union. The Liberian lawyer Alfred Brownell won the 2019 Goldman Environmental Prize for his work against palm-oil expansion.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; claims as reported by Zuckerman, with many sources named): Zuckerman, Planet Palm (2021), the chapters on Africa and Central America. The companies’ side was not examined here.

entries.label: Fred Kummerow, aged 98, petitions the FDA
entries.hint: The biochemist Fred Kummerow, who had warned of trans fats since the 1950s (see fats-1900-1960::th2), was still publishing at 98 in 2013 and petitioned the FDA to ban trans fats from the food supply; the agency’s late-2013 proposal was partly in response. Teicholz presents his career as a case of a researcher marginalised by industry and the American Heart Association; other accounts of his work are more cautious.
entries.note: SECONDARY (journalistic account, partisan): Teicholz (2014) ch.8. The petition and the FDA proposal of 2013 are in her text; her characterisation of the AHA’s role is hers.
